doc.title: Terri Lyne Carrington interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 9, 2003

title: Herbie Hancock and Jack DeJohnette
summary: She praises Herbie's openness, calls Jack DeJohnette a mentor she patterned herself on, and values reaction over signature licks.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: You said Herbie Hancock, going back to him for a moment, spoils you for playing with other people? Is that right?

Oh God, yeah. I mean he’s my favorite pianist. And he’s just so open and so receptive musically. He just reacts. He’s the kind of musician that I try to be as well so I really connect with his way because innately it was the same way I approached music even before I played with him. You know you’re really reacting to what you’re hearing. And you know you have the things that you can do but you don’t really just resort to the licks, resort to oh I know I can play this so let me play this, as well as like inspiration of the moment, based on what’s going on around you and then based on sometimes what you feel you have to do to inspire others as well at the moment. But not the kind of musician where I’ve developed this thing and I’m good at this thing so I’m going to kind of force this thing on you. That’s why Jack DeJohnette is one of my favorite drummers and has been a mentor to me over the years and I kind of patterned myself after him in many respects, especially when I was younger. To me that’s the kind of musician he is. He’s not a lick drummer but you know it’s Jack when you hear it because you know his sound, you know his touch, just his flavor but it’s not the licks that he plays. You know there’s a lot of drummers, they’ll play something and you know it’s them because they have signature things that they play.
